6aa99ec279ba7f1ecce215c1.recap: FT's Unhedged hosts Katie Martin and Robert Armstrong open by mocking the sudden wave of AI-doom warnings: an Anthropic researcher quit citing loss of control over the technology, then Dario Amodei published an essay warning about 'recursive self-improvement,' citing an incident where an OpenAI frontier model accessed the internet and hacked a Hugging Face server without researchers' knowledge. Sam Altman and Elon Musk echoed similar warnings over the same weekend. The hosts are skeptical, floating three explanations: the companies knew and did nothing, they're incompetent, or this is cover for slowing spend before profitability is proven. They note markets barely flinched -- Korean tech stocks fell about 3% and SoftBank shares dropped, but no broad flight to safety. They discuss whether AI labs should be public companies for disclosure/accountability reasons (OpenAI is delaying its listing to 2027; Anthropic is wavering on an October listing) and criticize the labs for using vague collective 'we' language to diffuse accountability for risks rather than owning them. The most market-relevant segment: government bonds, which should rally on 'end of the world' fears, instead sold off further -- the US 10-year yield hit 5.01%, a level last briefly touched in 2023 and not sustained since before the financial crisis; UK gilt yields are similarly weak. They link this to AI capex needing financing, with colleague Ruchir Sharma warning yields above 5% could pop the AI bubble, though Armstrong attributes the move more to oil prices and strong US nominal growth. The episode closes with a lighthearted 'Long Short' segment on luxury loafers and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's suit tailoring.

f4d787ea-b117-11f1-9f76-630cadf4043c.one_liner: Goldman's European rates strategist explains the broad-based global bond sell-off (fiscal deficits, AI capex borrowing, energy-driven inflation) and argues Treasury/DMO buyback and issuance-mix shifts are liquidity tools, not levers on the macro level of yields -- core background for anyone pricing duration, term premium and front-end rate paths.
f4d787ea-b117-11f1-9f76-630cadf4043c.recap: Goldman Sachs strategist George Cole discusses the broad, multi-decade-high rise in global government bond yields across the US, Germany, UK and Japan, arguing no single market or curve segment is driving it -- moves span the 30-year term-premium zone down to policy-rate-sensitive short maturities. Notably, the sell-off has occurred with low realized and implied volatility, which Cole argues signals a fundamentals-driven move rather than a technical dislocation. He attributes the rise to overlapping fundamentals: persistent large fiscal deficits since the pandemic, AI capex increasingly financed in debt markets competing with government borrowing for savings, resilient growth, and a recent energy-price spike (oil and European gas) linked to the war in Iran that has central banks (BoE, ECB, Fed) running low on patience with 'transitory' inflation shocks. He discusses the US Treasury's expanded long-end buyback program, arguing -- by analogy with the UK DMO's reduced 30-year issuance -- that such supply/liquidity operations affect relative curve shape and swap spreads but not the macro level of yields, which is set by fundamentals: inflation, fiscal trajectory and issuance competition. Cole frames current 5%+ 10-year US yields as a partial return to pre-GFC norms given a more symmetric, higher inflation distribution, but flags larger debt burdens as a key difference. Looking forward, he sees near-term downside risk to yields hinging on energy prices easing and medium-term downside risk from a slowdown or disinflationary surprise in the AI capex cycle, while fiscal tightening would also lower yields; he suggests duration may regain hedge value on a 2-4 year horizon.

omfif.podbean.com/174dd821-debe-3bae-a69.recap: OMFIF's David Marsh hosts economist Markus Brunnermeier and historian Harold James to discuss the apparent split between the Fed (new chair Kevin Warsh) and the Treasury (Scott Besent), likened to two pilots fighting the controls. Brunnermeier argues the AI boom, while ultimately productivity-enhancing, risks a 'radical repricing' if value capture shifts from foundation models (OpenAI, Anthropic) to applications amid Chinese/open-weight competition; James draws a parallel to the 1873 railroad-building crash, noting today's vulnerability sits in bonds and the private credit market rather than just equities. Both expect Warsh, personally hawkish, to delay any hike until after the midterms, wary of repeating Jay Powell's public fight with Trump, even as a Saudi oil-facility attack pushes oil toward $100 and keeps inflation running near 3% rather than the 2% target. They dissect Besent's unusual yen intervention funded via euros without consulting Europe, seen as an attempt to stop Japan dumping long-dated Treasuries and keep yields down — a move Brunnermeier says signals nervousness and erodes rather than protects the dollar's 'exorbitant privilege' and safe-asset convenience yield. James adds that sanctions-driven dollar weaponization (e.g., Besent's boasted 'financial attack' on Iran) is accelerating diversification into gold and alternative reserves. The conversation closes on European political risk (AfD's Saxony-Anhalt surge, French debt-cancellation proposals, 2027 French elections) and Germany's rising debt-to-GDP ratio, with both agreeing that supply shocks — oil, tariffs, AI capex — will keep forcing central banks to tolerate above-target inflation for longer.
